title: Lucia v. SEC (2018)
summary: Administrative law judges of the Securities and Exchange Commission are Officers of the United States who must be appointed under the Appointments Clause, and a party who timely objects to an unconstitutionally appointed judge gets a new hearing before a different judge.
notes:
Key line: Freytag says everything necessary to decide this case. (Justice Kagan)

Citation: 585 U.S. 237 (2018).

sections.Parties: The petitioners were Raymond J. Lucia and his firm, Raymond J. Lucia Companies, Inc., investment advisers charged by the Securities and Exchange Commission with fraud. The respondent was the Commission, but after the change of administrations the Government agreed with Lucia that SEC administrative law judges are officers, so the Court appointed Anton Metlitsky as amicus curiae to defend the judgment below. The presiding administrative law judge was Cameron Elliot, one of five SEC ALJs, all of whom had been selected by Commission staff rather than by the Commissioners themselves. The Court decided the case on June 21, 2018.
sections.Material Facts: The SEC may enforce the securities laws through administrative proceedings, which it typically assigns to an administrative law judge. Its ALJs receive career appointments to positions created by statute and hold authority to do all things necessary to conduct an adversarial hearing: they take testimony, receive evidence, rule on admissibility, enforce discovery, and issue initial decisions with findings of fact and conclusions of law. If the Commission declines review, it issues an order that the decision has become final and is deemed the Commission's action. Lucia marketed a retirement strategy called Buckets of Money using slideshow presentations that the SEC alleged misled prospective clients. The SEC charged him under the Investment Advisers Act and assigned Judge Elliot. After nine days of testimony and argument, Elliot issued an initial decision finding violations and imposing $300,000 in civil penalties and a lifetime bar from the investment industry. On review the Commission remanded for further findings, then affirmed the sanctions.
sections.Procedural History: Before the Commission, Lucia argued that Judge Elliot was an Officer of the United States who had not been appointed by the President, a court of law or a department head, so the proceeding was invalid. The Commission rejected the argument, holding that its ALJs are employees. A panel of the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit agreed. The en banc court divided evenly, leaving the panel decision in place, 868 F.3d 1021 (2017). Lucia petitioned for certiorari; the Solicitor General then switched positions and supported him, and the Court appointed an amicus to defend the judgment. Argument was heard on April 23, 2018, and the Court decided the case on June 21, 2018, reversing and remanding. Justice Kagan wrote for six Justices.
sections.Issue: Are the administrative law judges of the Securities and Exchange Commission Officers of the United States within the meaning of the Appointments Clause of Article II, section 2, clause 2, so that they must be appointed by the President, a court of law or the head of a department, or are they mere employees who may be hired by agency staff? If they are officers and Judge Elliot was not properly appointed, what remedy does a litigant who timely raised the objection receive, and may the same judge preside again after the Commission's ratification of his appointment?
sections.Holding: SEC ALJs are Officers of the United States. Under United States v. Germaine an officer must hold a continuing position established by law, and under Buckley v. Valeo must exercise significant authority pursuant to the laws of the United States. Freytag v. Commissioner, which held that special trial judges of the Tax Court are officers, controls, because SEC ALJs have equivalent duties and powers and, unlike special trial judges in major cases, can issue decisions that become final without further review. Because Lucia made a timely challenge to the validity of Elliot's appointment, he is entitled under Ryder v. United States to a new hearing before a properly appointed official, and that official must be a different ALJ or the Commission itself, since Judge Elliot cannot be expected to consider the matter as though he had not adjudicated it before. Reversed and remanded.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Kagan wrote that the sole question was whether the Commission's ALJs are officers or employees, and that the Court's precedents made elaboration of Buckley's significant authority test unnecessary because Freytag says everything necessary to decide the case. Special trial judges in Freytag held a continuing office established by law, and the Court found their authority significant because they take testimony, conduct trials, rule on evidence and enforce discovery orders, exercising significant discretion in carrying out important functions; that made them officers even in cases where their decisions were not final. SEC ALJs match point for point. Their positions are created by statute and filled by career appointment. They exercise the same four powers, and in one respect more: when the Commission declines review, the ALJ's decision becomes final and is deemed the Commission's action. The amicus argued that officer status requires power to bind the Government through final decisions, but Freytag rejected that argument when the Government made it, and the Court would not read Freytag differently now. On remedy, Kagan relied on Ryder, which gives a party who makes a timely Appointments Clause challenge the relief of a new hearing before a properly appointed officer. Because Judge Elliot had already heard the case and decided it, allowing him to rehear it would not create the incentive to raise Appointments Clause challenges that Ryder sought; another ALJ or the Commission must conduct the new hearing.

topics.lrs-s-officer-employee: The Court applied Freytag to SEC adjudicators without adopting an all-ongoing-statutory-duties definition.
topics.lrs-s-appointments-clause: The remedy turned on the ALJ not having been appointed by the Commission, one of the permissible appointing actors for inferior officers.
topics.lrs-s-article-ii-appointments: The case applies the text of Article II, section 2, clause 2 to agency adjudicators.

learning.separateOpinions: Seven to two on the judgment. Justice Thomas, joined by Justice Gorsuch, concurred, proposing that an officer is anyone who performs a continuing public duty under federal law, as the founding generation understood the term. Justice Breyer, joined by Justices Ginsburg and Sotomayor as to Part III, concurred in the judgment in part and dissented in part; he would have decided the case on the statutory ground that the Administrative Procedure Act requires ALJs to be appointed by the agency itself, warned that the constitutional holding raised removal-power problems, and objected to requiring a different ALJ on remand. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justice Ginsburg, dissented, arguing that officer status should turn on the power to issue final, binding decisions on behalf of the Government, which SEC ALJs lack.
